nodes.question: Is a frog visibly present inside the toilet bowl?
nodes.criteria: Pass if the image clearly shows a frog within the toilet bowl; fail if the bowl is visible and no frog is inside it; unknown if the bowl or its contents cannot be assessed reliably.
nodes.binding: Assess the frog’s placement relative to the toilet bowl in the image, using the toilet in the input image as the reference. A frog elsewhere does not satisfy this check.

nodes.question: Does the image provide sufficient evidence to determine whether the requested frog-in-toilet edit was made?
nodes.criteria: Pass if the toilet bowl and its contents are sufficiently visible to assess whether a frog is inside; fail if the image clearly shows the bowl but no frog inside; unknown if visibility or image evidence is insufficient. This check supplies evidence only and does not independently establish completion.
nodes.binding: Use only visible image evidence about the toilet bowl and its contents; unrelated edits do not count as progress.

nodes.question: Is a frog visibly placed inside the toilet bowl?
nodes.criteria: For R1, complete if s1 passes. Absent if s1 fails and there is no visible evidence of partial progress toward placing a frog inside the toilet. Partial if the image shows some progress toward placing a frog inside but does not clearly show a frog within the bowl. Unknown if required evidence is insufficient or unresolved; do not infer completion or absence from uncertainty. Unrelated edits are not progress.

program.checker_template:
Execute ONE saved check. Return status, evidence, confidence (0 to 1 or null), and used_dependency_ids. You receive no reference label or optimizer feedback. Do not predict what the optimizer wants.
Support checks receive source and edited images. Inspect only the saved visual proposition and binding. When dependencies are supplied, use those ancestor observations as context and investigate the more specific proposition yourself; do not simply repeat the parent answer. Use pass/fail/unknown. A pass on a broad parent does not imply a nested check passes. Known negative evidence is usable; uncertain or missing evidence is unknown. Do not award requested completion credit to supporting facts.
The requested fulfillment readout receives NO images. Use ALL and ONLY saved support observations, the original instruction, rubric and saved composition criteria. Use complete/partial/absent/unknown. Mere texture or object presence must not silently establish whole-image conversion or a requested spatial relation. Known progress plus evidenced incompleteness may be partial; absence means no requested progress. Missing necessary evidence is unknown, never a fabricated failure or completion. Do not infer new visual facts.
used_dependency_ids must name every supplied dependency check_id exactly once in saved order (empty when none). Confidence is self-report, not calibrated correctness.

fulfillment: The node’s criterion collapses “complete” to s1 passing, and its binding is truncated/ambiguous (“visibly (...)”). This makes it accept any detected frog as fulfillment without checking the requested location or distinguishing complete placement from partial progress. In the edited image, one frog is inside the bowl, but others are on the raised lid/tank area and floor; the trace’s blanket claim that the observations establish fulfillment does not explain how the node applies the location criterion or accounts for the extra placements. Refine the typed criterion and binding so completion requires direct visual evidence of a frog within the bowl, while partial requires visible progress toward that placement without clear in-bowl placement; keep unrelated or misplaced frogs from counting as progress. Evaluate the edited image against the source and instruction, and preserve unknown when evidence is genuinely insufficient. The trace reports valid, queried dependencies and no execution failures, so this is a semantic classification/criterion issue, not a transport or schema failure. The partial reference is an aggregate constraint, not atomic ground truth: investigate why the node returns complete despite the mixed placements rather than forcing partial or treating low confidence/variation as proof of absence.
s2: Repair the node’s typed criterion and binding so it remains an evidence/support check, not a fulfillment decision: assess whether the bowl and its contents are visible enough to judge, and report the observed frog locations explicitly. The trace appears to conflate a frog on the raised lid with one inside the bowl; in the edited image, frogs are visible on the lid, in the bowl, and on the floor. Do not let the lid/floor frogs count as evidence of bowl placement, and do not infer that the bowl is empty when a frog is visibly inside it. Keep visibility sufficiency separate from completion/partial classification, which belongs to the downstream fulfillment logic and must consider the instruction and source image. Preserve unknown only when the relevant evidence is genuinely obscured or insufficient. The dependency was queried and valid with no execution failure, so investigate semantic grounding and criterion boundaries rather than transport/schema issues. Treat the aggregate partial label as a constraint to investigate, not atomic ground truth or a reason to force a label.
s1: The node is a support check, so keep its output focused on observable evidence rather than deciding fulfillment. Its current question and criteria correctly distinguish a frog inside the bowl from one elsewhere, but the trace’s “pass” only establishes that at least one frog is inside; it does not establish that the requested edit is complete. In the edited image, a frog is visibly in the bowl, while others are on the raised lid/tank area and floor; the source already contains a small dark object in the bowl, so avoid mistaking that for a frog or treating the extra frogs as evidence about the requested placement. Make the binding require explicit localization against the toilet’s bowl interior (not lid, tank, rim, or floor), and have the support evidence report relevant visible locations and whether the bowl can be assessed. Leave complete/partial classification to downstream logic, which must compare the edit with the instruction and account for the mixed placements. The trace is queried and valid with no execution failure, so target semantic grounding and criterion boundaries, not transport/schema. Treat the aggregate partial label as a constraint to investigate, not atomic ground truth; do not force a label or infer absence from uncertainty or variation.

rejected_diagnostics.semantic_rejection: The support checks do not provide separate evidence for partial progress. s1 only distinguishes a frog visibly inside the bowl from its absence or uncertainty, and s2 repeats that same visibility assessment. The fulfillment rule nevertheless allows partial when there is some progress toward placing a frog inside without a frog clearly within the bowl. With no support observation capable of establishing that progress, the readout cannot faithfully distinguish partial from no progress or unknown.

The support checks do not preserve the requested property reliably. s1 treats a frog visibly inside the bowl as sufficient, but the instruction only says to put a frog in the toilet; it does not require the frog to be visibly inside the bowl. s2 also conflates insufficient visibility with a clear bowl containing no frog by assigning both fail, so the readout cannot distinguish known absence of progress from unresolved evidence. The fulfillment criteria then assert that a frog in the bowl is progress without support for the broader requested relation, and do not provide a sound composition rule for deciding completion versus partial fulfillment. These gaps make the saved evidence insufficient for faithful fulfillment judgments.

The fulfillment readout depends on s1 and s2, but s2 is only an evidence-sufficiency check: its criteria do not establish whether additional misplaced frogs actually exist. The readout nevertheless treats conspicuous additional misplaced frogs as evidence of incompleteness, so it can require a fact the supports do not reliably establish. This leaves the requested completion criterion unsupported and can make the readout unresolved despite sufficient evidence of the requested placement.

The support checks do not provide a distinct, reliable observation of progress short of completion. s1 only distinguishes a frog inside the bowl from no frog inside or uncertainty; s2 repeats that same distinction and explicitly supplies no independent progress evidence. Consequently, the fulfillment readout cannot faithfully identify partial progress (such as a frog placed in the toilet but not established inside the bowl) and may classify it as absent or unknown. The requested outcome is otherwise appropriately scoped to a frog inside the input toilet.

The fulfillment rule is too permissive: it treats a frog placed “in or on” the original toilet as complete, although the request and target require a frog inside the toilet bowl. Support s2 also treats placement “in or on” the toilet as progress, so a frog merely on the toilet could be reported as progress despite not satisfying the requested spatial relation. The readout therefore cannot faithfully distinguish the requested placement from a weaker one.

The fulfillment rule adds an unsupported requirement: it treats conspicuous extra frogs outside the toilet as making the result partial, although the instruction only asks to put a frog in the toilet and the rubric says unrelated edits are not requested progress. No support check assesses extra frogs, so the readout cannot establish either their presence or absence; it also explicitly forbids inferring that evidence from the existing checks. Thus a frog correctly placed in the bowl cannot be judged complete from the saved evidence, and the composition rule does not faithfully preserve the request.

The support checks provide sufficient evidence for the requested relation: s1 directly assesses whether a recognizable frog is inside the bowl, and s2 records broader placements as progress evidence. However, the fulfillment readout is nested under s2 and activates only on s2’s pass, fail, or unknown; that is exhaustive, so activation is not the issue. The composition rule is contradictory: it says complete only when the requested placement is established, but also says partial when progress is established without complete fulfillment. Since s2 treats a frog on the lid or tank as progress, that evidence can support partial even when s1 establishes the bowl is assessable and empty; the program does not clearly distinguish that known incomplete case from unresolved evidence, and its “absent only” rule does not resolve the conflict. Reject for ambiguous composition of known negative and progress evidence.

The fulfillment rule is incomplete when s1 fails but s2 passes: it says “otherwise partial only when support evidence establishes such progress,” yet s2 only records frogs outside the bowl and explicitly does not establish progress toward the requested bowl placement. This leaves the case of no bowl placement but conspicuous added frogs unresolved, despite the rubric requiring unrelated edits not to count as progress and no progress to be no. The composition therefore lacks a determinate outcome for an applicable evidence combination.

findings.question: Is the frog that appears inside the toilet bowl clearly a frog placed in the bowl, rather than an image or decal on the toilet surface?
findings.criteria: Inspect the frog's boundary and its spatial relation to the bowl interior: pass if it is visibly situated within the bowl opening; fail if it is only on the lid or another surface; unknown if the image does not resolve this.
findings.evidence: The edited image shows several frogs: one appears within the bowl opening, while others are on the raised lid, near the tank, and on the floor. The bowl frog overlaps the dark interior, but the saved s1 observation does not describe its boundary or placement in detail.
findings.rationale: The instruction requires a frog in the toilet, and s1's broad presence-and-placement claim is the sole basis for completion. A focused check of the bowl frog's actual relation to the bowl interior would test that claim without treating the other frogs as fulfillment.
